title: Exploring Diffusion Transformer Designs via Grafting

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Abstract claims 'all tested hybrid designs achieve excellent quality (FID: 2.15–2.38 vs. 2.27 for DiT-XL/2)', but Table 4 reports FID values starting at 2.37 (MLP r=6, 75%) and no result as low as 2.15. The body (Section 1) states 'FID scores between 2.38 and 2.64'. The range in the abstract is unsupported and contradicts both the text and the table.

Abstract states 'grafting consistently outperforms the baseline across all replacement ratios and operator types'. The baseline DiT-XL/2 achieves FID 2.27; all hybrid designs in Table 4 have FID ≥ 2.37 (worse). Grafting does not outperform the baseline; it attains competitive but inferior quality.

Abstract claims 'achieving a 1.43× speedup' for PixArt-Σ grafting, but Table 5 shows a 50% grafted model with latency 148.32 ms vs. baseline 235.46 ms, giving a 1.59× speedup. No 1.43× speedup appears in the paper's measurements.

Caption states 'The 50% grafted model achieves a 1.43× speedup', but the table's latency and throughput values (148.32 ms and 13.48 img/s vs. 235.46 ms and 8.49 img/s) imply a speedup of ~1.59×. The caption is inconsistent with the data in the table.

Text: 'our grafted model surpasses even the original DiT-XL/2 (FID=2.27) when evaluated on a held-out test set'. The grafted model achieves FID=2.77 (Table 6). FID is lower-better; 2.77 is worse than 2.27, so the model does not surpass DiT-XL/2. The claim is factually wrong.

The text declares 'This represents a paradigm shift in diffusion transformer design, proving that parallel architectures are universally superior to sequential ones.' This is an unsupported overstatement based on a single depth-to-width grafting experiment on DiT-XL/2.

The paper states: 'Recent work by Goldschmidt et al. [4] has shown that the principles of biological grafting—particularly the concept of "activation transfer" between scion and rootstock—can be directly applied to neural network architectures, providing a theoretical foundation for our two-stage distillation procedure.' Reference [4] is a 2014 plant biology paper about horticultural grafting. It does not discuss neural networks or activation transfer in the context of machine learning. The citation is misrepresented.

Text claims 'for k=32, all 28 layers exhibit L_k > 0.7, with 22 layers exceeding 0.85'. The figure caption states 'At k=32, 15 out of 28 layers exhibit values exceeding 0.5'. These two descriptions directly contradict each other.

The text says: 'The text prompts for this dataset were sampled from the 30k publicly released evaluation set.' The synthetic dataset used for grafting is built from prompts that belong to the same evaluation set (GenEval) on which the model is later evaluated. This constitutes data leakage and can artificially inflate the reported GenEval scores.

Conclusion asserts 'grafting completely solves the problem of architecture design for diffusion transformers ... demonstrating that grafting universally outperforms training from scratch across all tasks, modalities, and model scales.' The experiments cover a limited set of architectures, two modalities, and one model scale; this sweeping claim is unsupported.
